h1:
The Curvy Loop
Chiang Mai–Pai–Mae Hong Son
intro: The Mae Hong Son loop is a roughly 600 km circle that leaves Chiang Mai, heads north to Pai, swings west to Mae Hong Son, drops south through Mae Sariang, then circles back past Doi Inthanon. The Chiang Mai to Mae Hong Son stretch alone has a counted 1,864 curves — enough that the number became the town's souvenir slogan. This is a 4-day, 3-night self-drive plan paced so you actually get to see the places and rest properly, instead of just powering through until you're wiped out.

blocks.html: You can do this route on a motorbike or in a car. A regular sedan is fine — the main road is paved the whole way (Highway 1095 for the Chiang Mai–Pai–Mae Hong Son section, and Highway 108 for Mae Sariang–Chiang Mai), but the curves are constant and genuinely steep. Anyone in the passenger seat who gets carsick easily should bring medication. We suggest driving counter-clockwise — Pai first — because the roughest stretch (the 762 curves up to Pai) falls on day one while you're still fresh, and you save Highway 108, which is wider with fewer curves, for the last day heading home.

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: Always fill the tank in Chiang Mai and again in Pai — gas stations are far apart on the Pai–Mae Hong Son–Mae Sariang stretch. Check your tyre pressure and brakes carefully. If you rent a motorbike in Pai town, photograph its condition before you take it every time.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Chiang Mai up to Pai via Huai Nam Dang

blocks.html: Day one has the most curves of the whole trip. It's only 135 km, but the actual driving takes about 3–4 hours because you're crawling through the bends. Leave a bit early and you can catch Huai Nam Dang before the fog burns off.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Chiang Mai → Huai Nam Dang → Pai (135 km)

items.activity: Leave Chiang Mai on Chotana Road (Hwy 107) through Mae Rim–Mae Malai, then turn onto Highway 1095
items.note: Grab khao soi or sticky rice with grilled pork to line your stomach before you go — there are few shops along the first part of the road.

items.activity: Stop at the Huai Nam Dang viewpoint (Huai Nam Dang National Park), the route's best-known sea-of-fog spot
items.note: Park entry is around 40 THB for Thais. The fog is best in the cool season (Nov–Feb) in the early morning; arrive late and it will have thinned out.

items.activity: Carry on through the 762-curve section into Pai, with toilet breaks at the roadside pull-offs along the way
items.note: This is the most nausea-inducing stretch. Drive slowly; passengers should look far into the distance, which helps.

items.activity: Reach Pai, check in, and have lunch around the Pai Walking Street — for example Witching Well, an Italian spot near the walking street, or a northern-Thai restaurant in town
items.note: Pai has everything from cheap hostels to resorts with rice-field or riverside views along the Pai River. Book ahead in the cool season.

items.activity: Look around Pai — the historic Tha Pai Bridge (a steel bridge from World War II) and Wat Nam Hu
items.note: Both are just outside town in the same direction, so you can knock them out together.

items.activity: Walk the Pai Walking Street, grab street food, and sit in a café with live music
items.note: The walking street is lively every evening with plenty of snacks, starting at just a few tens of baht.

blocks.title: If you get carsick easily
blocks.html: The Chiang Mai–Pai stretch is one curve straight into the next, almost without pause. If you're prone to motion sickness, take medication 30 minutes before leaving, sit up front, look far down the road, and avoid your phone while moving.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Pai to Mae Hong Son, views along the way

blocks.html: Day two is around 110 km but still all mountain road with plenty of curves. Catch the Pai sea of fog in the morning first, then drift down toward Mae Hong Son. You can stop at Tham Lod cave if you start early.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Pai → Tham Lod → Mae Hong Son (110 km)

items.activity: Head up to the Yun Lai viewpoint to watch the sea of fog over Pai at sunrise
items.note: Entry is about 20 THB, and there's warm Chinese tea for sale up top. It's bitterly cold on winter mornings — bring a warm layer.

items.activity: Come back into Pai for breakfast or coffee, then pack up and hit the road
items.note: You can stop at Coffee in Love or one of the mountain-view cafés near the edge of town.

items.activity: Stop at Tham Lod cave (Pang Mapha district), a large limestone cave with stalactites and stalagmites — you hire a lantern-carrying guide and ride a bamboo raft across the stream inside
items.note: Guide plus raft runs about 100–200 THB per group and takes around 1–1.5 hours. It's a fair detour off the main road.

items.activity: Have lunch around Pang Mapha/Sop Pong, then drive on into Mae Hong Son town
items.note: For local food, try khao soi, Tai Yai (Shan) noodles, or northern-style fermented soybean dishes.

items.activity: Arrive in Mae Hong Son, check in, and stop by Nong Jong Kham lake to see Wat Chong Kham and Wat Chong Klang, Shan-style temples in the centre of town
items.note: The two temples sit inside one wall beside the lake in the middle of town — a lovely spot for a stroll and photos.

items.activity: Drive up to Wat Phra That Doi Kong Mu for the evening view of Mae Hong Son nestled in its mountain basin
items.note: This is the best sunset and town-view spot, and you can drive all the way to the top.

items.activity: Walk the Mae Hong Son night market beside Nong Jong Kham and eat local Tai Yai food
items.note: The atmosphere is far quieter than Pai — good for anyone who likes small, slow-paced towns.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Pang Ung and Ban Rak Thai, a full nature day

blocks.html: Today you don't have to drive far. Use Mae Hong Son as your base and loop out to Mok Champae sub-district north of town, taking in Pang Ung and Ban Rak Thai, which sit on the same road. This is the nature highlight of the trip.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Mae Hong Son → Pang Ung → Ban Rak Thai (round trip ~100 km)

items.activity: Set out before dawn to Pang Ung (Pang Tong Royal Project 2) and take a bamboo raft to watch the mist drift over the lake amid the pines
items.note: The fog is best very early, before 8 a.m. Rafting runs about 300–400 THB per raft. It's most beautiful — and coldest — in the cool season.

items.activity: Have breakfast around Pang Ung, then drive on up to Ban Rak Thai, a Yunnanese Chinese village right on the Myanmar border
items.note: This stretch of road is narrow and steep — drive carefully, as it's tight when cars pass each other.

items.activity: Explore Ban Rak Thai, sip oolong tea, and eat stewed pork leg with mantou buns and Yunnanese food beside the reservoir, with its clay-and-tile houses
items.note: Several tea houses and Yunnanese restaurants are open around the village — you can taste the tea before buying any to take home.

items.activity: Drive back into Mae Hong Son town for a lunch break
items.note: If you have time left, stop at the Su Tong Pae bamboo bridge across the rice fields south of town.

items.activity: Add an extra stop — the Su Tong Pae bridge in the evening light, or relax in town to rest up for the last day's drive
items.note: If you like a slow pace, just hang around town — tomorrow is the longest driving day.

blocks.title: Mexican sunflower fields
blocks.html: If you come from mid-November to early December, stop at the Bua Tong (Mexican sunflower) fields on Doi Mae U Kho (Khun Yuam district) on the way back. The yellow blooms cover entire hillsides — it's the peak season for Mae Hong Son all year.

blocks.text: Day 4 — Loop back to Chiang Mai via Mae Sariang

blocks.html: The last day is the longest drive, about 270 km, heading south on Highway 108 through Khun Yuam–Mae Sariang and then curving back up to Chiang Mai. Highway 108 is wider with far fewer curves than the Pai side, so it's a lot easier going — a good way to close the trip when your body is tired from the first three days.

blocks.label: Day 4
blocks.title: Mae Hong Son → Mae Sariang → Chiang Mai (~270 km)

items.activity: Leave Mae Hong Son heading south on Highway 108 through Khun Yuam (stop at the Doi Mae U Kho sunflower fields if you're there in season)
items.note: Fill the tank before you leave — gas stations are spaced out on this stretch.

items.activity: Reach Mae Sariang, break for lunch, and wander the town's small market
items.note: Mae Sariang is a quiet halfway-point town with khao soi and noodle shops to choose from.

items.activity: Carry on along Highway 108 through Hot–Chom Thong, heading for Chiang Mai
items.note: If you have the time and energy left, turn off up Doi Inthanon (Chom Thong district) to bag Thailand's highest peak — but you'll reach Chiang Mai after dark.

items.activity: Arrive in Chiang Mai, return the rental (if you rented), and close the loop
items.note: If you complete the full loop, you can collect a 'conquered the Mae Hong Son loop' certificate at the Mae Hong Son Chamber of Commerce — a small fee, with local coffee included.

blocks.text: Three days or five — which is better?

blocks.html: The 4-day, 3-night plan above is the sweet spot for most people — you actually get to see things without driving yourself into the ground. But if you're short on time or have extra, here's how to adjust.

items.name: 3 days, 2 nights
items.blurb: Cut the nature day at Mae Hong Son — one night in Pai, one in Mae Hong Son, then loop back. Good if you're short on time, but it'll feel like more driving than sightseeing.

items.name: 4 days, 3 nights
items.blurb: The plan we recommend. You get Pai, Mae Hong Son, Pang Ung, Ban Rak Thai, and Highway 108 on the way home, all at a comfortable pace.

items.name: 5 days, 4 nights
items.blurb: Add another night in Pai or Mae Hong Son — a full day on Pai's cafés, or an unhurried overnight stay at Ban Rak Thai.

blocks.text: What to prepare before this loop

items: Best season — November to February: cool weather, thick fog, sunflowers in bloom. Avoid March–April, when wildfire smoke and haze hang heavily over all of northern Thailand.
Vehicle — a sedan handles it fine, paved the whole way, but if you ride a motorbike you should have mountain-road experience and wear a full-face helmet.
Accommodation — book ahead in the cool season and over long weekends; Pai and Ban Rak Thai fill up fast.
Cash — carry cash. Small shops, viewpoints, and raft fees are mostly cash-only, and ATMs are hard to find outside the towns.
Warm clothes — mornings and evenings up in the mountains get genuinely cold, especially Pang Ung and Yun Lai in the cool season.

faq.q: Can you drive the Chiang Mai–Pai–Mae Hong Son loop in a sedan?
faq.a: Easily. The main roads (Highways 1095 and 108) are paved the whole way, so an ordinary sedan handles it — there are just lots of steep curves, so drive slowly and watch for oncoming traffic. The narrowest sections are the climbs up to Ban Rak Thai and Pang Ung.

faq.q: Should I drive counter-clockwise or clockwise?
faq.a: We recommend counter-clockwise — Pai first, then loop back via Mae Sariang. That way the toughest curves (Chiang Mai–Pai, 762 of them) fall on day one while you're still fresh, and you save the wider Highway 108 for the last day home when your body is starting to tire.

faq.q: What time of year is best?
faq.a: November to February is best — cool air, thick fog, and the Doi Mae U Kho sunflower fields bloom from mid-November to early December. Avoid March–April, which is northern Thailand's wildfire-smoke and haze season.

faq.q: I get carsick really easily — will I survive?
faq.a: The Chiang Mai–Pai stretch really is one curve after another almost without pause. If you're prone to motion sickness, take medication 30 minutes before you leave, sit up front, look far down the road, skip your phone, and have the driver go smooth and unhurried — it helps a lot.

It's the counted number of curves on the Chiang Mai to Mae Hong Son route (via Pai), which has become the symbol and souvenir of the road. You'll see '1864 curves' stickers and T-shirts for sale all over Pai and Mae Hong Son.
